title: Creating Suspense
summary: How to build tension in a Paper 2 story — delay, isolation, pace, sound, short sentences and punctuation for effect — with a step-by-step plan and a 350+ word sample story.

blocks.text: **Suspense** is the tense, uncomfortable — but enjoyable — feeling of not yet knowing. The reader senses that something is about to happen, it is probably bad, and the writer refuses to say what it is. That feeling keeps the reader reading.

Suspense is **not the same as action**. A chase can be fast and still have no suspense at all. Suspense comes from **delay**: the gap between the moment the reader senses danger and the moment the danger finally arrives (or turns out to be nothing). Every technique on this page is a way of opening that gap and holding the reader inside it.

In the exam, suspense is a skill you use **inside your Paper 2 story** (Section B Writing, 25 marks, about 35 minutes). Themes such as an unexpected event, a journey that goes wrong, being lost or alone, or a mystery all need it — and even a realistic story about a competition or a new skill becomes more gripping with a suspenseful climax. Controlling pace and tension is exactly what the top band of **Structure of texts** rewards, and varying sentences for effect is rewarded in **Grammar and punctuation**. Section A Reading also often asks how a writer builds tension, so this skill pays twice.

rows: Delay / slowing down time
He reached for the handle. Stopped. Listened. Reached again.
The reader is forced to wait, exactly like the character.
Withholding information
Something moved behind the shelves, but he could not see what it was.
Curiosity: the reader needs to know.
Short sentences
Silence. Then a click.
Like quick heartbeats. They speed up the pace.
One-line paragraphs
Then he heard it.
White space makes the reader pause and hold their breath.
Gradually building pace
Long, calm sentences at the start → shorter and shorter as fear rises
The reader feels the tension climb step by step.
Strong action verbs
He lunged for the door; the torch skidded across the floor.
Urgency and energy.
Sounds and onomatopoeia
Tap… tap… tap.
The reader hears the danger before seeing it.
Darkness, isolation and setting
a locked school at night, a power cut, a desert road with no signal
No help and no escape = more fear.
Time pressure
Three per cent battery. One bar of signal.
A countdown makes every second matter.
Physical signs of fear
His mouth was dry; his heart thudded against his ribs.
The reader feels the fear through the body (show, don't tell).
Rhetorical questions / dilemmas
Run back? Hide? Or wait?
The reader asks: what would I do?
Figurative language
Lockers lined the walls like silent soldiers.
Ordinary objects become threatening.
Red herring
A tall, faceless shape under the light — only a raincoat on a hook.
A false clue keeps the reader guessing.
Foreshadowing
He did not notice that the library door had been left unlocked.
An early hint creates unease.
Dramatic irony
The reader knows the caretaker has locked the gate. The boy does not.
The reader worries for the character.
Cliffhanger / twist
"So who turned on the light in there just now?"
The reader is left with a final shiver.

blocks.text: **Punctuation that builds suspense** (learn these separately from sentence types):

rows: Ellipsis (…)
Incomplete information, suspense or a pause, interruption
Tap… tap… tap.
Single dash (—)
Emphasis, interruption in the middle of speech
It came from the end of the corridor — slow, steady and getting closer. / "Who's th—"
Pair of dashes
Always extra information
whoever — or whatever — was out there
Colon
List, explanation, emphasis or extra information
There was only one way out: the fire exit.
Question mark
The character's (and reader's) questions
Was someone there?
Exclamation mark
Sudden shock, a shout
"Run!"

blocks.text: 3. How to build a suspense scene — step by step

items: **Start normal and calm.** Give the reader a safe, ordinary moment first (rain on the window, a quiet library). Fear only works if there was calm before it.
**Change one thing.** The light goes out. A sound stops. Someone is missing. The first sign that something is wrong.
**Isolate the character.** Take away help: no people, no phone, no light, no way out.
**Add a sound or sign — then delay.** A noise, a shape, a message. The character freezes. Slow time right down: describe heartbeats, breath, hands.
**Raise the stakes in steps.** Each paragraph closer, louder, darker. Sentences get shorter. Paragraphs get shorter.
**Offer a dilemma.** Hide or run? Answer or stay silent? Let the reader feel the choice.
**The reveal (climax).** Show what the danger is. It may be real, or a red herring that turns out harmless.
**Release, then a final twist (optional).** Let the reader relax… then leave one small question or shiver at the end.

rows: 1. Calm opening
Ordinary situation. Setting. The character relaxed
Longer, flowing sentences
2. Something changes
The first sign: darkness, silence, a missing person
A one-line paragraph to mark the change
3. Isolation
Help disappears. Time pressure starts
Mix of medium and short sentences
4. The threat approaches
Sound, shape, signs. Physical fear. Dilemma
Short sentences, fragments, ellipsis, one-line paragraphs
5. Climax / reveal
The truth: danger or red herring
A sudden, sharp sentence — then explanation
6. Resolution + twist
Safety, relief, maybe humour. Then one final unsettling detail
Sentences lengthen again. The last line is short

blocks.title: The pace ladder
blocks.text: Write the calm opening in long sentences of 20+ words. In the build-up, use 10–15 words. At the climax, drop to 1–6 words. After the reveal, let them grow again. Markers notice this control immediately — it is pace used for effect.

groups.title: Calm before the storm
items: Everything seemed perfectly ordinary until…

For a while, the only sound was…

groups.title: First signs
items: That was when he noticed…
Something was wrong.
The silence felt different now.

Her mouth went dry.
Every muscle locked.

Run? Hide? Or…

blocks.text: **Timing in the exam.** Section B Writing has about 35 minutes. Use them like this:

rows: Read the task twice. Underline the theme and every bullet prompt. Plan with G.C.S.P.P. (Genre, Characters, Setting, Point of view, Plot) and jot a short note for each paragraph. Decide what the threat really is and where you will reveal it.
Write. Aim for at least 350 words (strong answers are often 400–550 words). Slow down at the climax: one second can take a whole paragraph.
Proofread: speech punctuation, capital letters, apostrophes, spelling of your ambitious words, tense slips and missing words.

blocks.title: Sample story — After the Bell (suspense, realistic fiction)
blocks.task: You have read an extract about two friends who are trapped in a lift during a power cut. Write a story about a character who finds themselves alone in a place that is usually full of people. In your story you should: describe the place and explain why the character is alone, build tension as something strange happens, and explain what the strange thing turns out to be.
text: The last thing Omar remembered was the rain. It had drummed softly on the library windows while he finished his history notes in the corner behind the tallest shelf, the one nobody ever visited. Warm, comfortable and very tired, he had closed his eyes for just a minute.
When he opened them, the library was dark.

He sat up so quickly that his book slid to the floor with a slap. The clock above the door said only twenty past six, but the sky outside was already so dark that it looked like spilt ink. No voices. No footsteps. No squeaking trolley of returned books. The only sound was the rain, heavier now, hammering on the glass like a thousand impatient fingers.
"Hello?" His voice sounded tiny, swallowed by the rows of shelves.
Nobody answered.
He checked his phone. Three per cent battery. One bar of signal, flickering. With trembling thumbs, he began to type a message to his father: I'm locked in the —
The screen went black.

Omar told himself to stay calm. The main doors would be locked, but the fire exit beside the computer room opened from the inside; every student knew that. All he had to do was walk the length of the corridor. Thirty metres. Maybe forty.

He stepped out of the library. The corridor stretched ahead of him, long and grey, the emergency lights glowing a weak green at each end. Lockers lined both walls like silent soldiers. His trainers squeaked on the wet floor, and every squeak echoed back to him twice.
Then he heard it.
Tap.
He stopped. The sound stopped.
Tap… tap… tap.

It came from the end of the corridor, near the fire exit — slow, steady and getting closer. Omar pressed his back against the cold metal of a locker. His heart was thudding so loudly that he was sure whoever — or whatever — was out there could hear it. Beneath the green light stood a tall, thin shape. It did not move. It had no face.
Omar's mouth was dry. Run back to the library? Hide behind the shelves? Or…
A torch beam exploded into his eyes.
"Omar Khaled? What on earth are you doing here?"

The shape beneath the light was only a raincoat hanging on a hook. The tapping belonged to the walking stick of Mr Fathy, the night caretaker, who was now staring at him in disbelief, a bunch of jangling keys in his other hand.

Ten minutes later, Omar was sitting in the caretaker's warm room with a glass of sweet tea, waiting for his father and laughing at himself. Mr Fathy, however, was not laughing. He was frowning at the security screen on his desk.
"Strange," he murmured. "I locked the library at four o'clock. So who turned the light on in there just now?"
blocks.marks: Strong answer — Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3
notes: Creation of texts 5/5: every bullet is answered — the place and why Omar is alone (paragraphs 1–3: he fell asleep behind the tallest shelf), building tension (paragraphs 4–15), and what the strange thing turns out to be (the raincoat and the caretaker's walking stick). The theme of being alone in a usually busy place is kept throughout ('No voices. No footsteps.'). The twist ending keeps the reader's interest to the very last line without cancelling the resolution.

Vocabulary and language 3/3: sound vocabulary (drummed, slap, squeaking, hammering, jangling) and onomatopoeia ('Tap… tap… tap.'). Precise verbs (swallowed, stretched, thudding, exploded). Figurative language chosen for mood — the rain 'like a thousand impatient fingers', the sky 'like spilt ink', lockers 'like silent soldiers'. Physical signs of fear (trembling thumbs, dry mouth, heart thudding) show fear without naming it.

Structure of texts 7/7: a calm opening → a sudden change ('When he opened them, the library was dark.') → isolation and time pressure (dead phone) → the threat approaching in one-line paragraphs → a dilemma → a sharp reveal ('A torch beam exploded into his eyes.') → release (tea, laughter) → a final twist. The pace ladder is clear: long sentences in paragraph 1, fragments and one-line paragraphs at the climax, longer sentences again in the resolution.

Grammar and punctuation 7/7: a full range of sentence types — complex (opening paragraph, 'His heart was thudding so loudly that he was sure…'), simple sentences balanced for effect ('He stopped. The sound stopped.'), compound ('The main doors would be locked, but the fire exit… opened from the inside'), compound-complex ('The clock above the door said only twenty past six, but the sky outside was already so dark that it looked like spilt ink.'), fragments for effect ('Three per cent battery.'). Varied starters (-ed/adjective list 'Warm, comfortable and very tired', prepositional 'With trembling thumbs', 'Beneath the green light'). Punctuation: ellipsis for suspense and incomplete information. A single dash for an interrupted message and for emphasis. A pair of dashes for extra information ('whoever — or whatever —'). A colon introducing extra information (the words of the message). A semicolon joining two related clauses ('opened from the inside; every student knew that'). Accurate speech punctuation. Consistent past tense with past perfect for earlier events ('had drummed', 'had closed').
Word structure (spelling) 3/3: ambitious words spelt correctly (emergency, trembling, disbelief, caretaker, murmured). Possessives correct (Omar's mouth, caretaker's room). No homophone errors.

blocks.text: **Why does the author use…? (all the effects you could write about this sample)**

items.q: Why does the author use ellipsis in 'Tap… tap… tap.'?
items.a: Possible answers: to create suspense — the reader waits between each sound. To show a pause, as if Omar is holding his breath and counting. To show the sound is slow and steady, getting closer. To show the information is incomplete — we do not know what is making the sound.

items.q: Why does the author use the single dash in 'I'm locked in the —'?
items.a: A single dash shows an interruption: the message is cut off when the phone dies, which shows Omar is now completely alone and builds suspense, because his father will not know where he is.

items.q: Why does the author use the pair of dashes in 'whoever — or whatever — was out there'?
items.a: A pair of dashes always adds extra information: here it adds the frightening idea that the thing might not be human, which increases Omar's (and the reader's) fear.

items.q: Why does the author use the simile 'Lockers lined both walls like silent soldiers'?
items.a: Possible answers: to show the lockers are in straight, regular rows (imagery). To make ordinary objects seem threatening, as if they are watching or guarding him. To create a tense, uneasy atmosphere. To show how Omar's fear changes the way he sees a familiar place. The alliteration of 'silent soldiers' adds emphasis.

items.q: Why does the author write 'Then he heard it.' as a one-line paragraph?
items.a: Possible answers: to mark a turning point. To make the reader pause and hold their breath. To speed up the pace. To withhold information — 'it' is not explained, so the reader is curious. To make the sentence stand out.

items.q: Why does the author use a series of questions in 'Run back to the library? Hide behind the shelves? Or…'?
items.a: Possible answers: to show Omar's panicked thoughts (a dilemma). To make the reader ask what they would do. To slow the moment just before the climax (delay). The final ellipsis leaves the choice incomplete and builds suspense.

items.q: Why does the author end with Mr Fathy's question?
items.a: Possible answers: to create a twist after the relief. To leave the reader with a final shiver (a cliffhanger feeling). To suggest that something strange really is in the library. To make the story memorable.

rows: Revealing the danger too early ('a monster was in the corridor')
Delay: sounds, shapes, signs — reveal at the climax
Action with no tension (everything happens in one fast paragraph)
Slow down: one second can take a paragraph
Every sentence short from the start
Start calm and long. Shorten as tension rises
Telling the fear: 'He was very, very scared.'
Show it: dry mouth, cold hands, frozen legs
Too many !!! and …… everywhere
One ellipsis or exclamation where it really matters
Gore and violence instead of suspense
Suspense is what you do NOT show. Keep it suitable and subtle
'It was all a dream' or no ending at all
A clear reveal, then an optional final twist

blocks.title: Suspense checklist
items: I began with a calm, ordinary moment.
I isolated my character and took away help (light, phone, people).
I delayed the reveal with sounds, shapes and physical signs of fear.
My sentences and paragraphs get shorter as tension rises.
I used ellipsis and dashes correctly and not too often.
I gave my character a dilemma before the climax.
My climax reveals the truth clearly, and every bullet is answered.
I kept the past tense and the same point of view all the way through.

items: التشويق مش أكشن — التشويق هو إنك تأخر الحاجة اللي القارئ مستنيها.
ابدأ هادي وعادي، وبعدين غيّر حاجة واحدة (النور طفى، صوت غريب، حد اختفى).
خلي الشخصية لوحدها: مفيش ناس، الموبايل فاصل، مفيش مخرج.

وريني الخوف في الجسم (بُقه ناشف، قلبه بيدق) بدل ما تقول he was scared.
لازم في الآخر تكشف الحقيقة وتجاوب على كل نقاط السؤال، وممكن تختم بلمسة غموض صغيرة.

items.q: Practice task: 'You have read an extract about a family whose car breaks down in the desert. Write a story about an unexpected event during a journey.' Bullets: where the characters are going and who they are · what unexpected event happens · how the situation is resolved. Write a short plan using the suspense steps.
items.a: G.C.S.P.P.: adventure with suspense. Yassin (13, narrator, nervous of the dark), his older brother Karim (overconfident driver) and a Bedouin guide. The road to the White Desert at sunset. First person. Whole story. Plan: (1) calm — music, jokes, golden dunes. (2) change — the engine coughs and dies, silence. (3) isolation — no signal, darkness falls, the temperature drops. (4) threat — lights on the horizon moving towards them, an engine growling, a shape on the dune. (5) reveal — the guide from the camp, who noticed they had not arrived. (6) twist — at the camp, the guide says he did not send anyone: 'Which lights?'

items.q: Rewrite to build suspense with short sentences and delay: 'She opened the door and saw her brother hiding behind it.'
items.a: Example: She reached for the handle. Stopped. Behind the door, something shifted — a soft, careful sound. She held her breath, counted to three and pulled. A pair of eyes stared back at her… and then her little brother burst out laughing.

items.q: Add physical signs of fear to: 'Hamza heard footsteps behind him.'
items.a: Example: Hamza heard footsteps behind him. The back of his neck prickled, and his mouth went dry. His fingers tightened around the strap of his bag until his knuckles turned white.

items.q: Write a three-line cliffhanger ending for: 'He looked under the bed and saw —'
items.a: Example: He looked under the bed and saw — nothing. Only dust and a single sock. Then, from somewhere above him, a voice whispered his name.

items.q: Punctuate for suspense, using an ellipsis and a single dash correctly: 'the door opened slowly there was someone standing in the dark'
items.a: Example: The door opened slowly… There was someone standing in the dark — someone who should not have been there.

items.q: Name four techniques that build suspense and explain one effect of each.
items.a: Possible answers: short sentences — speed up the pace like heartbeats. Withholding information — creates curiosity. Isolation — no help makes the danger worse. Time pressure — every second matters. One-line paragraphs — the reader pauses and holds their breath. Onomatopoeia — the reader hears the threat before seeing it.
